# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

## Revision 24 (keel-cloud spec 215, 2026-11-04)

The rows keel-e2e-eval spec 134's review moved (`specs/215-the-corpus-fits-the-cards/corpus-rewording.md`, Table 1), before -> after (rule):

- Importance: Following phone and video calls -> Lipreading when people turn away (`imp-moment`)
- Importance: Not being worn out by listening -> Staying fresh enough to keep listening (`imp-backwards`)
- Importance: Catching announcements in shops and stations -> Knowing who is talking in a group (`imp-moment`)
- Current solution: Missed a little, caught up quickly -> Missed only a little (`cs-joined`)
- Current solution: Caught the gist, missed the details -> Caught only the gist (`cs-joined`)
- Current solution: Lost the thread and mostly nodded along -> Missed most of it (`cs-joined`)
- Compatibility: Their phone was with them and online -> had their phone with them {asked: was your phone with you} + had their phone online {asked: was your phone connected to the internet} (two rows; the pick stays on the first) (`cmp-one`, `cmp-subject`)
- Relative advantage: Following more without asking anyone to repeat -> More of the talk followed without asking for repeats (`ra-one`)
- Adoption friction: Wear the glasses, paired to the phone -> Wear the caption glasses in conversations {asked: you'd wear the caption glasses in your conversations} (`af-one`, `af-ground`)

screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real choices, but the second option switches from 'I' to 'you' ('you send them') while the other two speak as me.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps or my roles leaks, and my pick of people I know by name is kept as I made it.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? People I know by name (I send each one their own link) / People I found with Keel (I pick a list from Contacts; Keel makes a link for each, and I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post one link where they already are; each signs in with Google, then is interviewed)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is stated, but the number beside it, 'median 4 days out of 7', sits inside my 4-to-7 range and reads as if I was right; the deciding count (4 of 7 against a bar of 5, 1 short) only appears down on the Frequency card.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on this page, and the cards' 'N of 7 · bar M of 7' lines take a second look: the Frequency card says the same split three ways, and Importance prints '7 of 7 put it in their two' twice.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence, Frequency and Current solution are my beliefs in my words with my 4-to-7 days, and Importance is clunkier ('five things... one of the two') but clearly the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what a split on Frequency means for AirCaps, for example whether to aim at the people who hit this daily or to sell on occasional use; 'What it measures' only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: The '7 people answered' count stays visible, but three beliefs are called 'Holding up' on seven people with no word that seven is a small sample.
screens.instead: Split on how often: 4 of 7 lose the thread 4+ days a week, 3 only 2-3 days (you needed 5 of 7). The problem is real for all 7 but not daily for everyone, so ask the 3 when it happens and price for the heavy users. Only 7 answered, so read this as a lean, not a result.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven cells, all for me, on a 0-to-7 axis with my bar marked at 6, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Prevalence and keeps my 'at least 8 in 10' and my 'lost the thread of a conversation with hearing people', but it says 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' and drops my segment's 'in the US who talk with hearing people every week', so the belief is recognisable but not quite what I typed.
screens.why_b4: It tells me prevalence is not my problem among these seven and sends me to how often and whether it matters, which matters because the stage page already showed Frequency splitting people.
screens.why_b5: n is visible throughout, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" stops a 7-of-7 result from reading as proof about the whole US segment.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week lost the thread of a conversation with hearing people in the last 7 days -- and drop '— the most recent time it happened' from the Asked line, since the gate is a plain yes or no.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits right beside the deciding count: 4 of 7 at or beyond my 4 days, against a bar of 5 of 7, 1 short.
screens.why_b2: The bar and the 7 people are plain, but the chart's axis starts at a 0 nobody could pick, and the legend 'what you said · at what you said · short of it' took me a second look to work out what each mark counts.
screens.why_b3: It is my Frequency belief and my 4 to 7 days out of 7, said with the question's own clause, 'lose the thread of a conversation with hearing people', which is how my wearers say it.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the split and sends me to the next card, but it does not tell me what a 2-to-3-days-a-week wearer means for the idea, for example that the glasses must earn their place on a weekly rhythm rather than a daily one.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, 7 of 7 counted, and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', so nothing is claimed beyond the seven who answered.
screens.instead: Drop '— the most recent time it happened' from the Asked line, since the question counts days, start the axis at 1, and say what 3 of 7 at 1 to 3 days means: many have this only some days a week, so the glasses must justify being worn on those days.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The caption says 7 people picked two each for 14 picks, my row is marked "the problem you named" with 7, and the strip puts the bar at 5 of 7, so all three read at once, though the doubled "Asked:" and the trailing "the most recent time it happened" are clutter.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Importance and the belief line uses my actor, my circumstance and my job words, so I recognise it as the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: The So line correctly says top two is not first place, but it never tells me what this means for AirCaps or what to do next, such as leading the pitch with following the talk or looking at why "Getting a word in" came second.
screens.why_b5: The n is visible and a lean is called a lean, but my row "Following and joining the conversation" is the whole job and contains the other rows (getting a word in, lipreading, knowing who is talking), so 7 of 7 was close to certain and the screen does not say so.
screens.instead: Holding up, 7 of 7, but a lean from 7 people, and your row is the whole conversation, so it contains the other rows. Getting a word in at the right moment came second (3); test that as its own row next time.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 6 of 7 said today's way falls short against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each rung shows its count, the line sits plainly between 'Missed only a little' and 'Caught only the gist', and the strip shows 6 for and 1 against out of 7 with the marker at 5, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar is all read at first look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is mine, but the belief and the stem say 'following what hearing people said at the table' and 'your last conversation', while I typed a group conversation that is too fast or too noisy, so it is recognisable but narrowed to a table in one place and loosened to any conversation in the other.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the gap is real and its size (3 got only the gist, 3 missed most of it), and that my glasses get judged against that gap in the next study, which is the concrete next step for a captioning product.
screens.why_b5: The 7 answered and 7 counted stay visible, it says outright that a small group is a lean, not a call, and nothing claims more than the 6 of 7 carry.
screens.instead: Ask it as 'Think of your last group conversation with hearing people' and say the belief in my words, 'following a group conversation that is too fast or too noisy', not 'what hearing people said at the table'.

screens.why_b1: The verdict "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7", and the line "Current solution held, 6 of 7; the 1 who said no" ties the number to the verdict again.
screens.why_b3: "Current solution" is my dimension, and the belief about following what hearing people say still falling short is my circumstance; "at the table" is my group-conversation occasion.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for AirCaps, for example whether single-sided-deafness users like Tomás are weaker buyers or should be dropped from the wedge, and the "When a line fails" header on a line that held gives no direction.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7, the single dissenter and the group count of 1 are all visible, and nothing claims more than one person's reason, though the "When a line fails" header on a held line is briefly confusing.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's end-seat trick shows that people deaf on one side have a free positional workaround that works most of the time; I did not type that, and it hints that my segment's edge is weaker at the table.
screens.instead: Current solution held, 6 of 7; the one who manages is deaf on one side only and sits at the end to keep everyone on his good side, so people with single-sided loss may need AirCaps less: check whether they belong in the day-one segment.

screens.why1: It's the first thing on the link and it checks whether I'm someone this is meant for, so it's obvious why it's asked here.
screens.why2: Plain to me: I talk with hearing people at work, in shops and with family every week, and I'd answer it straight away.
screens.why3: It's about my own week, and I know without guessing whether I talk with hearing people.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it and don't overlap, and a screener gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's own phrase 'talk with hearing people every week' and leaks no product, plan or labels to me.
screens.why6: Short and easy to hear, but 'I'll read 2 options' before a plain yes-or-no is a clumsy extra line where 'Yes or no.' would do, as §17 says for a screener.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I actually got lost in one of those conversations this past week.
screens.why2: 'Lose the thread' is exactly how I'd put it, when I miss a word, then a sentence, and suddenly everyone is laughing and I don't know why.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether that happened to me this week, at the dinner table or at work, so I can answer it from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, and the chips only belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this question.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product leaks through, but 'face to face' is dropped, so I might count a phone or video call where captions or other things change the picture.
screens.why6: It's one short sentence ending in 'Yes or no.', easy to catch in one go, especially with the words on screen too.
screens.why7: The gate asks about the problem (losing the thread), not the circumstance, so someone who kept up all week can truly say No; it has the two fixed answers in order and no escape, as the card requires.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose the thread of a face-to-face conversation with hearing people? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to losing the thread this week, it is obvious to ask on how many days that happened.
screens.why2: Losing the thread and hearing people are exactly how I would say it, so I can answer on first reading or hearing.
screens.why3: I know which days this week I sat in a noisy café or a fast meeting and lost track, so I can count them without guessing.
screens.why4: The buttons run one per day, from 1 to 7, with no zero after my yes, and I can't recall sits apart as the one escape.
screens.why5: It asks only about my conversations, in the words deaf people use, with nothing about a product or the founder's terms reaching me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with the day unit said once, then say a number from 1 to 7 and one escape, which I can hold after one hearing.
screens.why7: All seven options count days of the window, from 1 to 7, the unit is named, and the required I can't recall is the only escape; whether the founder's low splits the buttons is set by the founder's range, not this screen.

screens.why1: I have just said how many days I lost the thread, so asking which part I would most like made easier is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Most rows read easily, but 'staying fresh enough to keep listening' is not how I'd put it: I don't really listen, I watch and lipread, and what runs out is my energy for concentrating.
screens.why3: Every row is something I did in my last conversation with hearing people, so I can answer from that.
screens.why4: 'Following and joining the conversation' is the whole thing, and lipreading, knowing who is talking and getting a word in are all parts of it, so it swallows the other rows and I'd be torn between it and the specific one.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or the company reaches me, and the rows are about my own conversations.
screens.why6: It is one short question with five short options read as a list and one escape at the end, which I could take in once on the captions or the screen.
screens.why7: The own item is present, never first, with three other rows and 'None of these' at the first ask, but it is the whole job and holds the other rows, which bends the rule 'none the whole job, none holding another' and leans picks toward it.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Keeping up when people talk fast · Lipreading when people turn away · Getting a word in at the right moment · Knowing who is talking in a group · Keeping up your concentration to the end · None of these

screens.why1: After asking how often I lost the thread and what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last conversation actually went is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I'd read it twice: 'your last conversation' drops 'with hearing people' from the screens before, and 'at the table' assumes my last one was over a meal or a meeting, when it may have been at the shop counter or in the hallway at work.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my last conversation with hearing people went, but if it wasn't at a table I'd have to guess which one the question means.
screens.why4: The ladder is in my words and runs from nearly everything to nothing, with 'I can't recall' fitting as the escape, but 'Followed nearly everything said' and 'Missed only a little' are almost the same thing to me.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but 'at the table' narrows 'too fast or too noisy' to one dinner-table scene the founder never named.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short question and five short parallel options I can hold, then 'or say you can't recall'.
screens.why7: Every rung is on the one measure of how much I followed, best to worst, with a working first rung ('Followed nearly everything said') and an outright failure last, so the belief can be both supported and refuted, and the 'I can't recall' escape is the right one for an act no one else can do for me.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of it did you follow? Followed all of it · Missed a few words · Caught only the gist · Missed most of it · Could not follow it at all -- or say you can't recall.
